I get why you'd pick it, since lions and roaring go together like dough and a hot oven. But the LORD never mentions roaring here. He asks about hunting the prey for a lioness and satisfying the hunger of young lions (Job 38:39).

Hills are everywhere in this passage, but not here. The young ravens cry out to God (Job 38:41). Shouting at a hill would be like me yelling at a cold oven and waiting for it to bake. I've done it. The oven did not answer.

Crying out to the wind sounds poetic, but that's not what the text says. The young ravens cry out to God as they wander about for lack of food (Job 38:41). Crying out to the wind would be like leaving a message for a stranger on the wrong phone number. These little ones cry out to the right One.

explanations.answer: Job can't make him do that
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The LORD asks if the wild ox will consent to serve Job, stay by his manger at night, or plow the valleys behind him (Job 39:9-10). Each question points to the same answer: Job can't make him. I've had a hard enough time getting a cookie to stay in the shape I stamped it.

explanations.answer: Yes if Job feeds him first

Speedy ox, huh? I like that picture, but the text doesn't say it. The LORD asks, "Can you rely on his great strength?" (Job 39:11). Strength is the word. Speed isn't in the verse.

A staredown is a cool picture, but the text has something different. This horse "…laughs at fear, frightened of nothing…" (Job 39:22). He does not turn back from the sword. Laughing is the word.

explanations.answer: Job has nothing to do with it
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. The LORD asks, "Does the hawk take flight by your understanding…" and "Does the eagle soar at your command…" (Job 39:26-27). Each question points to the same answer: Job isn't the one behind it. The hawk's flight and the eagle's soaring don't come from his understanding or his command.

explanations.answer: Job taught them both to fly
explanations.explanation: That's a big claim, friend. The LORD asks if the hawk takes flight by Job's understanding (Job 39:26). He asks if the eagle soars at Job's command (Job 39:27). Those questions point to a no, so Job isn't the one directing their flight.

explanations.answer: They fly only when Job calls
explanations.explanation: If birds waited on our calls, I'd have a very quiet sky. The LORD asks if the eagle soars at Job's command (Job 39:27). He also asks if the hawk takes flight by Job's understanding (Job 39:26). The answer these questions point to is no. Job isn't the one calling the shots.

That would be a gentle ending, but it's not what the LORD says. He says, "Let him who argues with God give an answer." (Job 40:2). It's an answer He asks for. Job is about to give his response.
